prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val][adversarial] Feature matrix with long row headers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Capability" · longest unbreakable word 91px · one-line width 411px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 36px · one-line width 36px
  col 3: header "Team" · longest unbreakable word 44px · one-line width 44px
  col 4: header "Business" · longest unbreakable word 72px · one-line width 72px
  col 5: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 83px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 510px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 509px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"A plan-comparison feature matrix: readers check whether a capability exists in each of four plans (Free → Enterprise), so the primary task is scanning a row rightward and comparing the tick/dash pattern across plans, with the capability name as the anchor.","reading":"Readers enter on the left row header, read the capability phrase as a unit, then sweep across the four mark columns to find the first plan that includes it. Vertical comparison of the mark columns is secondary but matters for 'what does Enterprise add' questions. The four mark columns are read as a set, not individually.","groups":["Columns 2–5 (Free, Team, Business, Enterprise) form one visual family: same role (boolean presence), same content type (✓/—), same alignment, and they should share a similar width rhythm so the marks form clean vertical columns and the header row reads as a plan ladder.","Column 1 (Capability) stands alone as the row identifier and must be visually dominant over the mark family."],"keep_intact":["All four plan headers — 'Free', 'Team', 'Business', 'Enterprise' are single unbreakable words (36/44/72/83px), so their columns cannot be narrower than word+21px padding (57/65/93/104).","The longest unbreakable word in column 1 (91px) — column 1 must stay at least ~112px so no word overflows.","✓ and — marks must never be split or clipped; they need only a few px of text width, so their columns are governed by header width, not content."],"may_wrap":["Capability phrases in column 1 — they are multi-word noun phrases that wrap cleanly at spaces, and row height can absorb 2–4 lines without breaking row integrity.","Nothing else: the mark columns contain no wrappable text (headers are single words, cells are single glyphs)."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r2A: widths [188, 58, 66, 93, 104] · table 510×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2B: widths [184, 59, 67, 94, 105] · table 510×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2C: widths [180, 57, 68, 96, 108] · table 510×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}

log.raw: {"critique":[{"design":"r2A","good":"Widest Capability column of the three (188px), so the row headers break at the best points — 'Data residency in the / European Union' keeps the preposition with its phrase, and all four plan headers stay on one line with the ticks forming clean, aligned vertical columns. Row heights are the minimum achievable for this width (3 lines max).","problems":"The right side of the header row is visibly crowded: 'Business' and 'Enterprise' sit flush against their cell borders with zero breathing room, so the header band looks pinched at the table's right edge. The four tick columns are also unevenly spaced — mark centres land at roughly 29 / 91 / 169 / 267px, so the gaps grow 62 → 78 → 98px left to right, which makes the plan ladder read as accelerating rather than even.","cause":"Every spare pixel was given to col 1, leaving Business at exactly 72+21=93 and Enterprise at exactly 83+21=104 — the hard word+padding floor. Header widths therefore track header length with no slack, producing both the flush text and the widening inter-mark rhythm."},{"design":"r2B","good":"A sensible middle position: col 1 is still close to maximum (184px), every header fits on one line, and no word is clipped. Row heights and line breaks in col 1 match r2A except at the very longest phrases.","problems":"The 1px of slack added to each mark column is invisible — it buys no perceptible breathing room around 'Business'/'Enterprise' yet costs col 1 four pixels, which is precisely the column where width changes real line breaks. It reads as an average of the other two rather than a decision, and the header band still looks tight.","cause":"Leftover pixels were distributed one-per-column instead of being concentrated where a few px actually register (the two long headers) or where they reduce wrapping (col 1)."},{"design":"r2C","good":"The most comfortable header band of the three — 'Enterprise' at 108px finally has visible air on both sides, and the table's right edge no longer feels clipped.","problems":"Col 1 drops to 180px and this changes a real break: 'Data residency in / the European Union' now orphans the article and makes the shortest row header look ragged, while the taller phrases keep the same 3-line shape. The row header is the anchor readers enter on; trading its width for mark columns that hold a single glyph is the wrong direction, and the tick spacing becomes even more lopsided (Enterprise mark pushed to ~267px).","cause":"Mark columns were widened beyond their content need (96/108 vs 93/104 floors) at the direct expense of col 1, which is the only column whose width changes typographic quality."}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"r3-breathing-headers","change":"Start from r2A (the best of the three) and fix its one real flaw: take 6px out of col 1 and give 3px of slack to Business and 2px to Enterprise, plus 1px to Team, so no header word touches its border. Col 1 stays at 184 — one line break at most, only on the longest phrases — while the header band stops looking pinched at the right edge."},{"name":"r3-max-capability","change":"The opposite bet: push col 1 to its absolute maximum (190) and put every mark column at its exact word+padding floor (57/65/93/104). This is the cleanest row-header reading possible in 510px — fewest wraps, no orphaned articles — accepting that Business and Enterprise headers sit flush against their borders as a deliberate, consistent typographic edge rather than an accident."},{"name":"r3-even-ladder","change":"Keep col 1 near-maximum (186) but give each mark column 1px of uniform slack (58/66/94/105) instead of concentrating it. This tests whether a perfectly uniform +1 rhythm across the four plan columns reads tidier as a family than r2A's mixed slack, at the cost of 2px of capability width — the smallest possible sacrifice for a more even header band."}]}
